name: ECG heart rate
seoTitle: ECG heart rate Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: ECG heart rate: work out paper speed from the R-R interval and the beats per minute. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: paper speed is what the ECG heart rate calculator works out, and it gets there from the R-R interval and the beats per minute. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the ECG heart rate calculator work?
sections.html:
The ECG heart rate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports paper speed in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the R-R interval, the R-R interval (boxes) and the beats per minute (BPM).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the ECG heart rate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Paper speed=(1 ÷ 60) × beats per minute (BPM) × R-R interval
Type of box=60 × paper speed ÷ (R-R interval (boxes) × beats per minute (BPM))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take R-R interval = 30 mm, Type of box set to Small, Paper speed set to 25 mm/s and Beats per minute (BPM) = 10. The calculator returns R-R interval (boxes) = 150.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: R-R interval (boxes) = 150 should be roughly the size you expected from R-R interval = 30 mm and Type of box set to Small.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The ECG heart rate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the R-R interval and the beats per minute — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the ECG heart rate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns paper speed, derived from the R-R interval and the beats per minute. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the ECG heart rate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the R-R interval and the beats per minute, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter R-R interval in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. R-R interval opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports R-R interval (boxes) = 150. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the ECG heart rate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
